title: Big questions - and key logistical details - loom ahead of China-U.S. summit
gist: One week before Xi Jinping's Washington summit with Trump, US planning is behind schedule and restricted to 'perfect reciprocity', while the substantive agenda centers on the November 10 expiry of the rare-earths export-control truce and the parallel US chip-control delay, amid mutual accusations of cheating on rare earths, Boeing orders, FCC import bans and phosphate exports.

insights.claim: With a week to go before the US-China leaders' summit, interagency briefing materials and talking points for Trump were not complete, and planning remained behind schedule versus previous state visits because of competing agency agendas.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Low preparation raises risk of thin or improvised deliverables; temper expectations for detailed trade outcomes.

insights.claim: The US has offered Xi no more than 'perfect reciprocity', meaning programming and access not exceeding what Trump got in Beijing in May, which led Xi's team to drop a proposal for him to speak at a US university.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Signals a transactional, tit-for-tat US posture rather than a warming reset.
insights.locator: The U.S. has ceded no more

insights.claim: The White House planned a state dinner of about 100 seats, versus Xi's 200-person banquet in 2015; Beijing asked for more than half the seats to accommodate CEOs, drawing White House pushback.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Uncertainty over which Chinese executives attend limits potential investment announcements.
insights.locator: For this visit, the White House

insights.claim: The White House has encouraged China to bring entrepreneurs and executives to court Chinese investment, but Beijing had not finalized a list because of US planning uncertainty and because Xi does not usually travel abroad with business leaders.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Inbound Chinese investment deals at the summit look unlikely to be large.

insights.claim: Beijing wants certainty, not just negotiation, over every protocol detail of the summit, from seating and photographs to speaking time, and has privately complained about last-minute US planning.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Protocol friction is a leading indicator of summit atmospherics.
insights.quote: all of these things are something that Beijing will pay attention to and will want not simply to negotiate but will want to feel certainty about
insights.locator: Every meal, every moment they sit down

insights.claim: The moratorium on Chinese rare-earth export controls and the parallel one-year delay on US export controls on advanced semiconductor chips both expire on November 10.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Hard catalyst date: rare-earth, magnet and AI-chip supply chains face binary risk around November 10.
insights.locator: Another key issue on the table

insights.claim: China offered before Trump's May Beijing visit to extend the rare-earths moratorium to the end of Trump's term in January 2029, but the US rejected it and requested only a six-month extension, to be announced after Xi's visit, hoping to negotiate a better deal later.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: The US deliberately chose a short leash; expect recurring rare-earth deadline risk every six months rather than a multi-year truce.
insights.locator: Before Trump's visit to Beijing this past May

insights.claim: The US accuses China of violating the rare-earths truce through its total rare-earths export ban on Japan, where many US suppliers are located, and US companies still lack some export licenses for rare earths used in specialized magnets.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Rare-earth magnet supply remains constrained despite the truce; supports non-China rare-earth and magnet producers.
insights.locator: However, officials from both the U.S. and China

insights.claim: A senior US official called China's compliance on rare-earth exports very disappointing, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned the US would push back if China kept taking measures detrimental to US businesses.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Raises odds of US retaliation or tougher summit stance on rare earths.
insights.quote: We expressed our concern that the rare earths are not flowing as freely as they could
insights.locator: Scott Bessent, the U.S. treasury secretary

insights.claim: In August China's commerce ministry sanctioned the Responsible Business Alliance, a US supply-chain monitor that helps run a minerals audit program, chilling China's critical-mineral industry.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Supply-chain auditing of Chinese minerals is becoming harder, raising compliance risk for Western buyers.

insights.claim: China's ongoing export ban on phosphate, a key fertilizer ingredient that Beijing justifies by Iran-war shortages, is squeezing American companies.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Tight phosphate supply supports non-Chinese fertilizer producers and food-input inflation.
insights.locator: American companies have also been squeezed

insights.claim: China's spring commitment to buy at least 200 more Boeing planes has hit roadblocks, partly because the US is reluctant to sell spare parts for Boeing planes and for China's C919 airliner, which relies heavily on American and European parts.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Boeing's China order is at risk of slipping; aerospace parts are a live US lever over China's C919 program.

insights.claim: Chinese officials say the FCC's recent bans on importing Chinese drones, routers, inverters and robots violate the 'constructive relationship of strategic stability' framework, while a senior US official framed them as tools of Trump's reindustrialization agenda.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: US import bans create opportunities for non-Chinese makers of inverters, drones and networking gear.

insights.claim: A senior US official said China's recent State Council decrees blocking enforcement of sanctions, including US sanctions, are very disruptive to the promise of strategic stability.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Anti-sanctions legislation raises legal conflict risk for multinationals operating in China.
insights.quote: are all very disruptive to the promise of strategic stability
insights.locator: The official did say China's recent

insights.claim: China's main summit goal is less specific policy commitments than a broad spirit of 'constructive relationship of strategic stability', and Beijing hopes Trump will attend APEC in Shenzhen in November.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Beijing is incentivized to keep relations calm into November; lowers near-term escalation risk.
insights.locator: China's main goal will be less

insights.claim: Beijing is enthusiastic about summitry with Trump because it sees it as a way to manage the United States and is pleased with the direction of relations.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: China sees the status quo as favorable, implying it will trade stability for time.
insights.quote: I think that's one of the reasons why they want to sustain diplomacy with Trump is they're pretty happy with the direction things are going
insights.locator: I think that's one of the reasons

insights.claim: Companies and industry experts are pressing for US-China cooperation on guardrails for developing and using artificial intelligence, one of the summit's most pressing concerns.
insights.speaker: Emily Feng
insights.so_what: Any AI-safety bilateral language would be a new policy vector for AI firms.
insights.locator: One of the most pressing concerns
